analysis.investment_thesis: MOIL is a government-owned cyclical manganese ore miner with a trailing P/E of 64x on what appear to be severely depressed earnings — the classic cyclical trap Lynch warned about. With ROE at only 8.3%, no pricing power, and volatile earnings swinging from ₹478 Cr (FY19) to ₹251 Cr (FY23) and back, this is not the compounding growth story I look for.
key_strengths: Zero debt balance sheet with solid equity base of ₹2,638 Cr — one of the few genuinely clean PSU balance sheets
Near-monopoly on domestic manganese ore mining gives some structural protection; 64.7% government promoter backstop reduces existential risk
Operating CF positive all 5 years; FY25 OCF of ₹434 Cr shows underlying cash generation when commodity prices cooperate
key_risks: Classic cyclical trap: trailing P/E of 64x with forward P/E of 12.6x signals current earnings are severely depressed — we don't know where we are in the manganese cycle
ROE of only 8.3% is well below my 12% minimum threshold; a business with near-monopoly assets should earn far more on equity
Other income (interest on cash) was ₹317 Cr in FY15 vs shrinking rapidly since — the 'real' operating business has always been thinner than headline profits suggest
red_flags: Revenue over 10 years: ₹822 Cr (FY15) → ₹1,579 Cr (FY25) — that's barely 6.7% CAGR for a supposed growth story
Net profit is wildly erratic: 428→173→307→417→478→248→377→251→293→382 — no earnings predictability, which is death for PEG analysis
Implied TTM earnings (~₹104 Cr, derived from 64x P/E on ₹6,673 Cr market cap) vs FY25 reported ₹382 Cr suggests recent quarters have cratered — earnings quality unknown
analysis.detailed_analysis:
MOIL is a textbook cyclical commodity stock — the kind Lynch explicitly warned investors to handle differently from growth stocks. The P/E of 64x isn't cheap just because forward P/E is 12.6x; it means the market is banking on a massive earnings recovery in manganese prices tied to Indian steel demand. The PEG ratio framework breaks down entirely here: if trailing earnings are ~₹104 Cr (implied by 64x P/E on ₹6,673 Cr market cap) versus ₹382 Cr reported in FY25, something has gone badly wrong in recent quarters that the annual data doesn't capture. That disconnect — 84% implied earnings drop — is a flashing warning sign I can't ignore.

The financials confirm this is a business without a growth story. Revenue grew from ₹822 Cr to ₹1,579 Cr over a decade — roughly 6.7% CAGR — while profits are entirely hostage to manganese ore commodity prices. ROE of 8.3% on a company with ₹2,638 Cr in equity and near-monopoly mining rights is frankly embarrassing; a private operator would earn double that on the same assets. Capex is accelerating (₹216 Cr → ₹297 Cr over 3 years) but free cash flow remains thin and volatile. Government ownership at 64.7% means capital allocation discipline is suspect and management incentives aren't aligned with minority shareholders. I'd rather own a mid-cap specialty chemical company growing 20%+ with a PEG under 1 than a PSU miner riding commodity cycles at 64x earnings.
